definition.text: Discounted cash flow analysis values a security, project, company or asset by allowing for the time value of money in its expected cash flows.

facts.text: All future cash flows are estimated and discounted, usually at the cost of capital, and their sum is the net present value.
The discount rate combines the time value of money (the risk-free rate) with a risk premium for the chance the cash flows never arrive.
Run in reverse, taking a known price and solving for the rate, it gives the internal rate of return or a bond's yield.
It is widely used in investment finance, real estate development, corporate finance, actuarial science and patent valuation.
It has been used in the UK coal industry since 1801 and was first set out in modern terms by Irving Fisher (1930) and John Burr Williams (1938).
Its forecasts assume the future resembles the past, and small input changes, especially to terminal value, can swing the result greatly.
Traditional DCF counts only financial costs and benefits, leaving out environmental, social and governance performance.

definition.text: Integrated Future Value extends discounted cash flow and net present value to count the long-term value and risks of natural and social capital.

facts.text: It lets companies value investments for their long-term environmental and social returns as well as financial ones.
The social cost of carbon can be included to capture the damage to society from an investment's greenhouse gas emissions.
It supports Integrated Bottom Line decisions, which combine financial, environmental and social reporting in one balance sheet, going beyond the triple bottom line.

definition.text: Exponential discounting is a discount function in which value falls by the same proportion for each extra unit of delay.

facts.text: Total utility is the sum of each period's utility multiplied by the discount factor δ raised to the power of the time period.
The trade-off between consumption at two dates depends only on how far apart they are.
It is dynamically consistent: preferences do not change as time passes unless new information arrives.
It is the most common assumption in economics because of its simplicity, though alternatives such as hyperbolic discounting have more empirical support.
In finance, discounting is normally modelled as exponential.

definition.text: Discounted utility is how desirable a future event, such as consuming a good, looks from the present rather than when it happens.

facts.text: It is the present discounted value of future utility, smaller than the future utility for anyone who prefers sooner gratification.
The discount factor β lies between 0 and 1 and is sometimes explained as a person's patience.
Intertemporal consumption models maximise the sum of discounted utilities subject to a budget constraint on the present value of spending.
Tversky and Kahneman found people who choose 1 candy bar now over 2 tomorrow also choose 2 in 101 days over 1 in 100 days: inconsistent time preferences.

definition.text: Epstein–Zin preferences are a form of recursive utility that separates attitudes to risk from attitudes to substituting consumption over time.

facts.text: Recursive utility combines a time aggregator for preferences without uncertainty and a risk aggregator that sets the certainty equivalent of future utility.
A parameter β sets the rate of time preference and ρ sets the elasticity of intertemporal substitution, while α encodes risk aversion.
Unlike standard expected utility forms such as isoelastic utility, the elasticity of intertemporal substitution can be set independently of risk aversion.
Setting α equal to ρ gives back ordinary time-additive expected utility.

definition.text: The expected utility hypothesis holds that people choose between risky options by comparing the probability-weighted average of the utility of each outcome.

facts.text: It is a foundational assumption of mathematical economics about decisions under uncertainty, and rational choice theory builds on it.
Expected utility is the sum over outcomes of each payoff's utility times its probability.
The curve of the utility function captures risk attitude: linear for risk-neutral, convex for risk-seeking and concave for risk-averse people.
Bernoulli's version was the first formal statement of marginal utility: an extra sum is worth less to a rich person than a poor one.
Von Neumann and Morgenstern defined a rational decision-maker by four axioms: completeness, transitivity, independence and continuity.
Psychologists have found systematic violations, and behavioural finance has produced generalised theories such as prospect theory to account for them.
Such deviations are called irrational because they depend on how a problem is presented, not on its costs, rewards or probabilities.

title: St. Petersburg paradox
article: Expected utility hypothesis#The St. Petersburg paradox

definition.text: The St. Petersburg paradox is a coin-flipping game with an infinite expected payoff that people will nonetheless pay only a little to play.

facts.text: The prize doubles each time the coin lands heads, and the game ends at the first tails.
Someone caring only about expected value should pay any finite amount to play, but in reality few would pay more than $25.
Nicolaus Bernoulli described it in 1713, prompting expected utility theory as a solution.
Daniel Bernoulli's 1738 paper used it to argue that expected value theory must be normatively wrong.

title: Subjective expected utility
article: Expected utility hypothesis#Savage's subjective expected utility representation

definition.text: Subjective expected utility is Leonard Savage's framework showing that expected utility, with personal probabilities, can guide choice even when probabilities are not objectively known.

facts.text: Savage proved, from seven axioms, that expected utility can be used to make an optimal choice among acts.
Its key method is a focus on observable choices; psychology matters only as far as it changes choices.
Frank Ramsey's 1926 representation theorem was an earlier approach to subjective probability.
Savage concluded that people are neutral towards uncertainty and that observation is enough to predict the probabilities of uncertain events.

title: Preference reversal over lotteries
article: Expected utility hypothesis#Preference reversals over uncertain outcomes

definition.text: A preference reversal occurs when people value one lottery more when pricing it but choose the other when comparing them directly.

facts.text: Subjects price 'p bets' (high chance of a small prize) below '$ bets' (small chance of a big prize), yet usually pick the p bet head to head.
The effect was found in studies starting with Lichtenstein and Slovic in 1971.
Later work suggests the behaviour can fit neoclassical theory under specific assumptions.
